items.title: Cedwyn Film
items.summary: A film about Llandough village in 148 scenes.
items.content_html:
Cedwyn · the film releases a new scene every morning, with a planned running time of 4 h 56 min.

Behind each door, a scene of about two minutes: the people of Llandough talking over what is happening on paper and around the village, from before the deeds to today.

Every dated event in the chronology sits behind exactly one door, with its evidence numbers.

items.title: Tŷ Mawr: the Great House of Llandough
items.summary: The historic environment record lists Tŷ Mawr, beside the church of St Dochdwy, as the principal freehold of the parish, with details pointing to the seventeenth century.
items.content_html:
The historic environment record kept by Heneb, cited into the Cedwyn archive by the Royal Commission, lists Tŷ Mawr by the church of St Dochdwy at Llandough as the principal freehold holding of the parish. Details found in the house pointed to the seventeenth century.

The same record places the manor courts of Llandough and Leckwith at Tŷ Mawr. In 1908 the manor court remembered John Williams of Tŷ Mawr as “for many years a juror of the court”.

Around 1841 the tithe puts John Williams on 36 plots, the whole Tŷ Mawr holding. His granddaughter Mary (Nancy) Williams lived in the house until her death in 1983.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/wales/

items.title: 1824: the first record that names the house
items.summary: The earliest record found that names Tŷ Mawr is David Stewart’s survey of 1824. The family dates its arrival at the house to 1667.
items.content_html:
Tŷ Mawr is first named in the record found so far in David Stewart’s 1824 survey for the Bute estate (catalogue EV-0211): a description the estate wrote of itself, not a deed.

The Williams family dates its acquisition of Tŷ Mawr to 1667. The sources for that date are Mary Williams’ statement in the newspapers of 1974 and ITV News in 1988.

Documents dated before 1824 that come from the Bute estate or other third parties are not treated as records of Tŷ Mawr. Their application to the house is under examination, and they are tested rather than repeated.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/maps/

items.title: 1974: “an ancient Welsh house” and 1,700 names
items.summary: In April 1974 the national press reported an open day to save “an ancient Welsh house”, Tŷ Mawr, Llandough. Local history records 1,700 signatures on a petition that year.
items.content_html:
In April 1974 the national press reported an open day held to save “an ancient Welsh house”: Tŷ Mawr, Llandough.

Local history records that 1,700 people signed a petition to keep the house that year.

The house was demolished in 1988. Houses now stand on its yard, tithe plot 209.

items.title: What the courts decided, and what the record leaves open
items.summary: The High Court in 1986 and the Court of Appeal in 1987 decided possession and limitation. Paper title was not in issue.
items.content_html:
From 1955 to 1988 the family held the house through every court action brought against it, and has asked for the records ever since.

The High Court (trial 24 July 1986) and the Court of Appeal ([1987] EWCA Civ 2) decided possession and limitation in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler, in favour of the registered owner from 1982/83. Paper title was not in issue (catalogue EV-0074, EV-0080).

The Primary Record Register lists the questions each record still has to answer, such as what parcels and plan the 1955 possession order covered, and which issues fell outside the 1986–87 determination.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/records/

items.title: 46 records that should exist
items.summary: The missing records register lists 46 records that should exist. None is in the archive, and 19 were searched for and not found.
items.content_html:
The Research Library keeps a register of records that should exist but are not held: 46 at the last count. None is in the archive. 19 were searched for and not found.

Each one has a blank page with its own catalogue number, kept ready for the record. Among them: MR-0001, the instrument recording the 1667 acquisition of Tŷ Mawr by the Williams family; MR-0002, the 1877 agreement between the Bute trustees and Daniel Thomas & Son, with plan; MR-0003, the February 1916 yearly agricultural tenancy of the whole farm to John Williams, with plan.

Anyone holding one of these records can match it to its catalogue number.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/research/missing-records/

items.title: 1000 Cuts: a dated chronology, 1870s to 1988
items.summary: A dated chronology of the Williams family’s position at Great House Farm in law and in fact, each step linked to its evidence.
items.content_html:
1000 Cuts sets out the Williams family’s position at Great House Farm, in law and in fact, from the 1870s to 1988. Each entry gives a date, what happened, what it changed, and the evidence pages it rests on.

Every entry is graded by the strongest item it cites, from 1 (a record read in full) to 6 (research inference). Family testimony and open questions are marked as such.

It opens with John Williams of the Great House, for many years a juror of the Llandough manor court, which met in his house.

Read the record on Cedwyn: cedwyn.bucklerfamily.estate/thousand-cuts/

items.title: Cydwin, Cedwyn, Ty Mawr: every name the records use
items.summary: Great House Farm appears in the records under 26 different wordings, and Llandough under nine.
items.content_html:
The same farm appears in the records under 26 wordings, among them Cydwin, Cedwyn, and “Cydfin Farm or Ty Mawr Farm, (107 a.)”.

Llandough itself has nine, from Landoche-juxta-Cardif to Llandough juxta-Penarth.

The Nomenclature index gathers every name the records use for the same thing, so that a search under one name finds them all.

items.title: Lavernock Point, 11 May 1897
items.summary: From the cliff at Lavernock the first wireless messages crossed open sea, to Flat Holm and a week later to Brean Down. The guided tour stops there.
items.content_html:
On 11 May 1897, from the clifftop at Lavernock near Penarth, the first wireless messages crossed open sea: to Flat Holm, and a week later to Brean Down.

That spring the young Guglielmo Marconi came to the Severn Sea, the Welsh papers followed every step, and a Cardiff engineer, a Mr Williams, worked beside him.

Lavernock Point is one of nine stops on the Cedwyn Estate guided tour, which runs from the site of Tŷ Mawr at Llandough out to the point and back.
